title.en: The Two Friends Who Set Off to Travel Round the World

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Two Friends who set off to travel round the world', eBook #28932

summary.en: Two newly married men set out in opposite directions to travel round the world, so they might tell others what it is like. They live, have children, and grow old on the way; only in extreme age do they meet again, their drinking horns worn to stubs by the many fills along the road. 'The world is great indeed.'
summary.zh: 兩名新婚男子相背而行，分頭環繞世界，好向族人述說天下之貌。旅途遙遠，二人成家生子、白髮蒼蒼，直到垂暮方重逢，獸角杯已被沿途取水磨得只剩柄底。二人相語：『世界真是大啊。』

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo (Inughuit) oral tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s, published 1921. Colonial-era mediation acknowledged; no living-community consent claimed.

passages.text: Two men desired to travel round the world, that they might tell others what was the manner of it. This was in the days when men were still many on the earth and there were people in all the lands — the teller adds that now men grow fewer and fewer, evil and sickness having come upon them. The two had each newly taken a wife and had no children yet. They made themselves cups of musk-ox horn, each cutting his cup from one side of the same beast's head, and they set out, each going away from the other by different ways, agreeing to meet again some day. They travelled with sledges and settled each summer on whatever land they reached.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Two Friends who set off to travel round the world'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The journey took a whole life. On the road the two men had children, the children grew old, and the travellers became so old they could no longer walk but were led by their children. At last they met — and of their drinking horns there was but the handle left, so many times had they filled them by scraping the horn against the ground as they drank. 'The world is great indeed,' they said when they met. Young when they started, old when they found each other again, led by their children. Truly the world is great, the teller concludes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Two Friends who set off to travel round the world'; not verbatim.

title.en: Nukunguasik, Who Escaped from the Tupilak
title.zh: 努孔瓜西克逃出圖皮拉克之手

region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Nukunguasik, who escaped from the Tupilak', eBook #28932

summary.en: Nukunguasik stumbles on a brother of his neighbours secretly fashioning a tupilak monster to bite him to death. Creeping close, he slaps the maker's side and asks 'But where is this Nukunguasik?' — frightening the sorcerer dead at his own unfinished weapon. The reawakened tupilak later gnaws its maker's corpse, and the victim of the plot lives to be the oldest man of his place.
summary.zh: 努孔瓜西克偶然撞見鄰家兄弟暗中捏製圖皮拉克怪物，欲令其咬死自己。他悄近拍了那術士一掌，問道：『可努孔瓜西克在哪裡？』術士竟被自己未竟的咒物嚇死。復活的圖皮拉克其後啃食造主屍身，而陰謀所害之人卻壽終為故里最長者。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland (Ammassalik) oral tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Tupilak-making is a documented historical shamanic practice; tale presented as archival record, not as representation of living Ammassalik belief.

passages.text: Nukunguasik lived in a place with many brothers, a wifeless man to whom the brothers gave meat for the pot when they made a catch. One day he rowed northward in his kayak and, on a whim, crossed to a big island he had never visited. Going up to look at the beautiful land, he came upon the middle one of many brothers busy in a hollow, whispering all the time. Crawling stealthily nearer, he heard the whisper: 'You are to bite Nukunguasik to death; you are to bite Nukunguasik to death.' The man was making a Tupilak and stood telling it what to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nukunguasik, who escaped from the Tupilak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddenly Nukunguasik slapped the maker's side and said: 'But where is this Nukunguasik?' The man was so frightened that he fell down dead. Nukunguasik saw that the sorcerer had let the Tupilak sniff at his body — it was now alive and lay there sniffing — and being afraid of it, he went away without harming it. He rowed home, and the brothers waited in vain for the middle one to return. When they prepared to search for him, Nukunguasik suggested the island where no one ever goes, and sent the searchers to its southern side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nukunguasik, who escaped from the Tupilak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The brothers found the dead man and cried out over him — and there lay the Tupilak, still alive, nibbling at the body of its maker. The brothers buried him under a mound of stones and went home. Nukunguasik lived on as the oldest man of the place and died at last after many years. 'Here I end this story: I know no more,' the storyteller says. The tale teaches the old Greenlandic belief that a tupilak made to kill another may turn on its maker, and that the sorcerer who dies at his own creature dies doubly shamed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nukunguasik, who escaped from the Tupilak'; not verbatim.

title.en: Qujavarssuk: The Strong Man Protected by the Old Wizard
title.zh: 古亞瓦舒克：受老巫護佑的強者

region.zh: 西格陵蘭伊克舒阿峽（努克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Qujavarssuk', eBook #28932

summary.en: A childless strong man arranges with an old fisherman-wizard to beget a son on his wife; the boy Qujavarssuk grows to be a matchless hunter, harpooning two seals daily. When two jealous kinsmen raise a tupilak against him, the boy seems to vanish from its sight and lures it to destroy its own maker; his wife later banishes the sea-ice by magic. Named after a man who died of hunger, Qujavarssuk finally out-hunts the champion of Amerdloq and takes a whale.
summary.zh: 無子的強者與老漁巫立約，令其子嗣托生己妻；所生古亞瓦舒克日獵雙豹，技冠群倫。兩名嫉妒親戚以圖皮拉克加害，少年隱身使其撲空，誘其吞噬造主；其妻更以巫術破海冰。少年承亡者之名，終勝阿默德洛克第一獵手，獵得一鯨。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab (Nuuk) district oral tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Includes a ritual-wife arrangement described as the teller's community custom of its era; recorded as archival material without endorsement.

passages.text: A strong man lived at Ikerssuaq with one other resident, an old man who lived on nothing but devil-fish and traded the fish for the strong man's surplus catch. The hunter, who never failed to catch seal, fell silent as time went on, because he could get no children. The old one was a wizard, and one day the strong man bargained with him: go to my wife when she comes down to the shore, and each day I will give you something of my catch. The wife, finely dressed, went down twice before the old wizard came in to her; that day he caught scarcely any fish, and the strong man, hearing his confession, gave him a seal and sealed their bargain. The wizard then prescribed a cormorant skeleton from a bird cliff and an unsunned stone for a lamp, and told the couple the woman was with child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qujavarssuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The wife bore a son, whom the strong man gave to the old one to name after a dead man — for it was believed the qualities of the dead passed to the living namesake. 'Let him be named after him who died of hunger in the north, at Amerdloq,' said the wizard, and the boy was called Qujavarssuk. When the wizard tested the finished kayak by holding the boy in it, seals rose all around the water, a sign he would be a chief among hunters. Rowing out for the first time, he harpooned a black seal at his first cast, and every day thereafter he brought home a catch, two seals a day even when the ice pressed the open water into a narrow lead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qujavarssuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a time of hunger, visitors heard of Qujavarssuk and came to his land. Among them were two old wizards, his mother's kinsmen, who were fed on the best of the catch — but one of them took offence at being told he had begun eating from the wrong side of the seal, lest the hunter's luck cease. Laden with gifts on the road home, the angry kinsman resolved to make a Tupilak to eat Qujavarssuk. When Tugto's wandering wife, herself a greater wizard than her husband, was asked to magic away the blocking ice, she called a bear and a walrus as helping spirits, was carried out over the floes in their jaws, fought and groomed an old woman of the undersea, and returned with scratched cheeks; only when her sores healed did the wind loose the ice, and no one might hunt until five days had passed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qujavarssuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Tupilak paddled after Qujavarssuk, but each time he stepped into his kayak he vanished from its sight, and each evening he came home with two seals. Starving, it went on land — and struck its head on ground that had become a sheer cliff with Qujavarssuk standing plain on top; a great stone broke its rib; a black bird bit a hole above its flipper. Turning in fury on the man who had made it, the Tupilak coloured the water red with his blood — then, ashamed that all other Tupilaks would call it shameful to kill one's maker, it swam far out into the open sea and was never seen again. Qujavarssuk later moved to Amerdloq, out-hunted its champion, harpooned a whale that came in toward his house as he said the beasts he struck always did, and at last went home south and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qujavarssuk'; not verbatim.
